inline.s: Master Shandao said, “It is precisely because reciting the name is easy that continuity brings immediate rebirth. If one can keep the recollection of the Buddha uninterrupted from thought to thought, making it the task of a lifetime, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred. ...... May all people reflect deeply on this. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they must steel their minds and restrain themselves, and never neglect it by day or by night. When the previous thought ends in death, the next thought is born immediately. Forever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma-bliss, and even attaining Buddhahood — how joyful!”

[It is precisely because reciting the name is easy]This is because the practice of reciting the name of the Buddha is easier to accomplish than that of contemplating the Buddha. [Continuity brings immediate rebirth]When the moment of death arrives, as long as one’s thought of reciting the Buddha remains continuous (not interrupted by stray thoughts), one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Master Yinguang said:

“The practice of Buddha-recitation should take the Pure Land scriptures and commentaries as the standard. Sentient beings in the last age are heavy with karma and deeply hindered; even those who practice contemplation as taught in the Contemplation Sutra find it hard to succeed. That is why most of the patriarchs of the Lotus School have specifically advocated reciting the name. Because reciting the name is easy,
continuity brings immediate rebirth
(From “The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang · Reply to the Seventh Letter of Layman Ding Fubao”) [Making it the task of a lifetime]One who practices in this way for the whole of his life.

[Steel the mind and restrain oneself]“Steel the mind” means to rouse one’s mind to do what ought to be done; “restrain oneself” means to hold oneself back from doing what ought not to be done. These four characters, “steel the mind and restrain oneself,” are a powerful weapon for overcoming difficulties and sweeping away obstacles.
[Never neglect it by day or by night]Neither by day nor by night should one stop the continuous recollection from thought to thought.
Question:
Master Shandao teaches:
“continuity brings immediate rebirth.”
What does this mean?
Answer: “Continuity brings immediate rebirth” means this:
when the moment of death arrives, the thought of reciting the Buddha remains continuous
(not interrupted by stray thoughts)
, and one is immediately reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The “continuity” spoken of here is the thought of reciting the Buddha continuing from thought to thought, with no stray thought mingled in the midst (if a stray thought is intermingled, it is no longer continuity). One must on no account misconstrue the two characters “continuity” here as the name of the Buddha being recited aloud continuously (while stray thoughts are nonetheless mingled in the mind). This is the very meaning of “a hairbreadth’s error leads to a thousand miles of difference.”

Question: How do we know that “continuity brings immediate rebirth” means that when the moment of death arrives the thought of reciting the Buddha is continuous and one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and not that as long as in ordinary life one has at some point kept the recollection continuous, one will be reborn there at the moment of death?
Answer: Master Shandao teaches:
“If one can keep the recollection of the Buddha uninterrupted from thought to thought,
making it the task of a lifetime
(one who practices in this way for the whole of his life)
, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred.”
Please note
“making it the task of a lifetime,”
not one who in ordinary life merely kept the recollection continuous for a time. Master Shandao went on to teach:
“May all people reflect deeply on this. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they must steel their minds and restrain themselves, and never neglect it by day or by night
(neither by day nor by night should they stop the continuous recollection from thought to thought)
when the previous thought ends in death, the next thought is born immediately
. They will forever enjoy the unconditioned Dharma-bliss, and even attain Buddhahood — how joyful!”
Therefore, “continuity brings immediate rebirth” means that when the moment of death arrives the thought of reciting the Buddha is continuous and one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Question: How do we know that the “continuity” in “continuity brings immediate rebirth” is “the thought of reciting the Buddha remaining continuous,” and not “the name of the Buddha being recited aloud continuously (while stray thoughts are nonetheless mingled in the mind)”?
Answer: “Continuity brings immediate rebirth” comes from Master Shandao’s Treatise on the One and the Mixed Practice of Pure Karma, which says:

Question: Why not have them practice contemplation, but instead direct them to single-mindedly recite the name? Answer: Because sentient beings are heavy with hindrances; the object [of contemplation] is subtle while the mind is coarse, consciousness stirs and the spirit flies, so contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore the Great Sage
(Śākyamuni Buddha)
, out of compassion, directly urged single-minded recitation of the name.
It is precisely because reciting the name is easy
(that is, precisely because reciting the name is easier to accomplish than contemplating the Buddha)
that continuity brings immediate rebirth

(that is, when the moment of death arrives, as long as one’s thought of reciting the Buddha remains continuous (not interrupted by stray thoughts), one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
. If one can keep the recollection of the Buddha uninterrupted from thought to thought, making it the task of a lifetime
(one who practices in this way for the whole of his life)
, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred.
Why is this so? Because there is no external defiling condition
and so right mindfulness is attained
(a mind that no longer grasps outwardly after sundry things achieves right mindfulness)

, and because this accords with the Buddha’s fundamental vow, does not violate the teachings, and complies with the Buddha’s words. But if one discards single-minded recollection and practices mixed karma, then among a hundred, one or two at best may succeed; among a thousand, three or four at best. Why? Because the defiling conditions stir and agitate
(because the mind grasps outwardly after sundry things)
and so right mindfulness is lost
, because it does not accord with the Buddha’s fundamental vow, because it violates the teachings, because it does not comply with the Buddha’s words,
and because the mindfulness is not sustained and continuous
and because the mind is not continuous in mindful gratitude for the Buddha’s grace

. Though one performs karmic deeds, they always accord with fame and gain, and one delights in approaching defiling conditions, thereby obstructing oneself and obstructing others’ right practice for rebirth. May all people reflect deeply on this. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they must steel their minds and restrain themselves, and never neglect it by day or by night;
when the previous thought ends in death, the next thought is born immediately
. They will forever enjoy the unconditioned Dharma-bliss, and even attain Buddhahood — how joyful!”
(From Master Shandao of the Tang dynasty, Treatise on the One and the Mixed Practice of Pure Karma; for a detailed explanation see
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teachings

Notice the expressions Master Shandao uses in this passage: “keep the recollection uninterrupted from thought to thought,” “right mindfulness attained,” “right mindfulness lost,” “the mindfulness is not sustained and continuous,” “the mind is not continuous,” and “when the previous thought ends in death, the next thought is born immediately.” All of these make clear that the “continuity” in “continuity brings immediate rebirth” is “the thought of reciting the Buddha, continuous from thought to thought,” not “the name of the Buddha being recited aloud continuously (while stray thoughts are nonetheless mingled in the mind).”
Master Yinguang greatly admired this passage, saying

“Venerable Master Shandao was an incarnation of Amitābha, endowed with great spiritual powers and great wisdom. In his grand exposition of the Pure Land, he did not prize the mysterious and subtle, but simply taught people to practice at the level of sincerity and plain reality.
As for the one and the mixed practices he set forth, the benefit is without limit.
(From “The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang · Reply to the Letter of a Certain Layman of Yongjia’s Kinsmen”)
Master Tanluan said:
with no other thought intermingled
(there being no other thought mixed in)
, thought following thought up to ten recollections,
this is called the continuity of the ten recollections
(From A Brief Treatise on the Meaning of the Land of Peace and Bliss) Therefore,
continuity is having no other thought intermingled
(no other thought being mixed in).
Master Daochuo said:

“When all sentient beings are in the moment of death, the wind-blade undoes the body, the suffering of death presses in, and great fear arises. Therefore, upon meeting a good friend [in the Dharma], one gives rise to great valorous effort,
thought after thought continuous
through ten recollections, which is the augmentation of a superior root of goodness, and one attains rebirth.”
(From the Collection on Peace and Bliss) Therefore,
continuity is the continuity of thought after thought, not continuity of the mouth
Regarding “keeping the recollection uninterrupted from thought to thought,” the
Master Yongming, who was the reappearance of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
“At the time of walking the path
(the meditative walk)
and paying homage, while reciting the Buddha and making the vow, with earnest and utmost sincerity,
free of all stray thoughts
, as one about to meet a death sentence, as one shut in a prison
(bì prison: a jail)

, pursued by hostile bandits, pressed by water and fire, with a single mind seeking deliverance, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly to realize the unborn, to liberate sentient beings widely, to continue and promote the Triple Gem, vowing to repay the four kinds of grace — with such wholehearted sincerity, what is done will surely not be in vain. If words and deeds are not in accord, and the power of faith is slight, without
a mind of uninterrupted recollection from thought to thought
, but with the intent to be constantly interrupted
(the thought of reciting the Buddha being cut off by stray thoughts)
, relying on this indolence, though one hopes for rebirth at death, one will only be shielded by karmic hindrances, and will likely be hard put to meet his good friend
(likely unable to meet a good teacher who could give rise to his right mindfulness at death)
; pressed by wind and fire, right mindfulness will not be accomplished. Why is this?
Now is the cause; death is the result
. The cause must be real, and then the result will not be false. If one wishes
to accomplish the ten recollections at death
, one must prepare in advance the means of crossing, gather together one’s merit, and dedicate it to this time
(dedicate it to the moment of death)
, the recollection not being in the least deficient
(achieving the uninterrupted recollection from thought to thought)
, then there is nothing to worry about.”
(From The Collection of Myriad Goods Returning to the One)

In this passage Master Yongming clearly points out that “without a mind of uninterrupted recollection from thought to thought, but with the intent to be constantly interrupted” is the same as “words and deeds not being in accord, and the power of faith being slight,” and is precisely indolence. Therefore,
continuity is an unbroken recollection from thought to thought within the mind
, not a continuity of the mouth

[Accomplishing the ten recollections at death]Accomplishing the continuity of the ten recollections at the moment of death. [Preparing in advance the means of crossing]“Means of crossing” refers to ferries and bridges; “preparing in advance the means of crossing” means making thorough preparations beforehand.
The twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Chewu, taught:
“What is called upholding the name is to hold it fast and pressing it to the breast
(holding it firmly in mind)
; this means holding it firmly in the mind and never forgetting it for a moment. Should there be
a single thought of interruption
, then it is no longer upholding. Should there be
a single thought of mingling
, then it is no longer upholding.
Uninterrupted from thought to thought, with no mingling and no interruption
, this is true vigor. When vigor knows no stopping, one gradually enters single-minded undistracted concentration, and perfectly accomplishes the pure karma.”

(From The Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu) This is to say: when the thought of reciting the Buddha is not cut off by stray thoughts and is not mingled with stray thoughts, this is called uninterrupted recollection from thought to thought.
Therefore,
uninterrupted recollection from thought to thought is without the mingling of stray thoughts.
[Hold it fast and pressing it to the breast(
yīng

)]“Hold it fast” means to grip tightly without letting go, extended to mean earnest and affectionate; “pressing to the breast” means to keep it engraved in the mind. “Holding it fast and pressing it to the breast” describes earnestly and affectionately bearing something in mind without forgetting.
As for what constitutes the continuity of the ten recollections, Master Tanluan gives instruction in A Brief Treatise on the Meaning of the Land of Peace and Bliss(see
Master Tanluan’s Pure Land Teachings
for details):

[For example, suppose a person is in a desolate, open place and encounters hostile bandits who draw their swords and, with bold valor, come straight at him to kill him. The man runs swiftly and spies a river. If he can cross it, his life can be preserved. At that time he thinks only of the means of crossing: “When I reach the riverbank, should I cross clothed or unclothed? If I cross clothed, I fear I shall not get across; if unclothed, I fear I shall have no time.” Having only this thought and nothing else at all, the single thought of how to cross the river is precisely that one thought.
A mind thus unintermingled is called the continuity of the ten recollections.

Answer: Suppose there is a person in the wilderness who encounters hostile bandits who draw their swords and charge at him to kill him. The man runs for his life and sees a great river. If he can cross it, he can preserve his life. At that time he thinks only of how best to cross: “When I reach the riverbank, should I swim across clothed or unclothed? If clothed, I fear I shall not make it across; if unclothed, I fear I shall not have time.” At such a moment he has only the thought of crossing the river and nothing else; he has but the single thought — how to cross the river? — which is that very thought. A mind thus unintermingled with other thoughts is called the continuity of the ten recollections.
[So too with the practitioner: he recollects Amitābha Buddha, just as that man thought of crossing, and goes straight
(same as “straight”)

through the ten recollections: whether recollecting the Buddha’s name, or recollecting the Buddha’s marks, or recollecting the Buddha’s light, or recollecting the Buddha’s spiritual powers, or recollecting the Buddha’s merits, or recollecting the Buddha’s wisdom, or recollecting the Buddha’s fundamental vow.
With no other thought intermingled, thought following thought up to ten recollections, this is called the continuity of the ten recollections.

The practitioner likewise, with a single mind recollecting Amitābha Buddha, just as that man with a single mind thought of how to cross the river, goes straight through ten recollections: whether recollecting the Buddha’s name, or the Buddha’s marks, or the Buddha’s light, or the Buddha’s spiritual powers, or the Buddha’s merits, or the Buddha’s wisdom, or the Buddha’s fundamental vow. With no other thought intermingled, thought following thought up to ten recollections, this is called the continuity of the ten recollections.
[Following]In succession.
Question: What does “when the previous thought ends in death, the next thought is born immediately” mean?

Answer: This means: because the recollection is continuous from thought to thought, the last thought at the moment of death is necessarily a thought of reciting the Buddha, and immediately after that last thought one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Question: It is said that Master Shandao maintained that reciting the name certainly leads to rebirth, and even that he maintained that “as long as there is faith, one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death.” Is this so?
Answer: As for how rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is attained, Master Shandao makes it perfectly clear in the passage above:
“continuity brings immediate rebirth

(that is, when the moment of death arrives, as long as one’s thought of reciting the Buddha remains continuous (not interrupted by stray thoughts), one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
And he admonishes:
“If one can keep the recollection of the Buddha uninterrupted from thought to thought, making it the task of a lifetime
(one who practices in this way for the whole of his life)
, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred.
May all people reflect deeply on this. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they must steel their minds and restrain themselves, and never neglect it by day or by night.”
This is the guiding principle of practice for the Pure Land school!

How could it be that he maintained that reciting the name certainly leads to rebirth, or even that “as long as there is faith, one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death”? Moreover, according to the records, Master Shandao copied the Amitābha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha more than one hundred thousand fascicles in his lifetime, which shows that he held that sutra in the highest veneration and practiced in accordance with its teachings. In that sutra the Buddha says that through faith, vow, and recitation of the name with single-minded undistracted concentration, one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death. How could Master Shandao have gone against the Buddha’s instruction and said that “reciting the name certainly leads to rebirth,” or even that “as long as there is faith, one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death”? Therefore,

statements such as “Master Shandao maintained that reciting the name certainly leads to rebirth; Master Shandao maintained that as long as there is faith, one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death; ...” were all fabricated by later people and imposed upon Master Shandao, falsely claiming this to be his Pure Land thought. In fact, if you simply set Master Shandao’s teaching on “continuity brings immediate rebirth” and his teaching on the “right and sustaining practices” side by side with this so-called “Master Shandao’s Pure Land thought,” you can clearly see that, while they raise the banner of “relying upon Master Shandao,” they are in fact opposing him head-on, by quoting out of context and distorting his original words.

Question: Since they do not truly believe in Master Shandao, why do they raise the banner of “relying upon Master Shandao” and claim that “as soon as faith is roused, one is reborn,” “reciting the name certainly leads to rebirth,” “the gate of the great vow,” and so on, are his Pure Land thought?

Answer: Because if people knew that such statements as “as soon as faith is roused, one is reborn,” “reciting the name certainly leads to rebirth,” “the gate of the great vow,” and so on were their own, then, since these statements clearly depart from the meaning of the scriptures, people would sniff at them in derision, and all the less believe them. But if, by quoting out of context and distorting Master Shandao’s original words, they falsely claim this to be his Pure Land thought, and then go on to say, “Since Master Shandao is an incarnation of Amitābha, his thought
is tantamount to what Amitābha Buddha himself proclaimed
.” In this way they can deceive the faithful, and no one will dare to criticize or oppose them.
Question: What is
“the right and sustaining practices”?
Answer: This is Master Shandao’s instruction
on how the Pure Land school should practice
. The master said
As for right practice: to practice specifically in accordance with the rebirth scriptures — this is called right practice. What are these?
With a single mind
specifically recite and read this Contemplation Sutra, the Amitābha Sutra, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and so on;
with a single mind
specifically contemplate, observe, and recollect the glorious rewards of that land. If bowing, then
with a single mind
specifically bow to that Buddha; if reciting aloud, then
with a single mind
specifically recite that Buddha; if praising and making offerings, then
with a single mind
specifically praise and make offerings; this is called right practice. Further, within this right practice there are two kinds: first,
with a single mind

specifically recite the name of Amitābha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of the length of time, without letting go thought after thought — this is called the right conclusive karma, because it accords with that Buddha’s vow; if one relies on bowing and recitation and so on, this is called sustaining karma. Apart from these right and sustaining practices, all other good deeds are called mixed practices. If one cultivates these right and sustaining practices, the mind is constantly drawn near, recollection never interrupted — this is called being without interruption.”
(From
Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles

Translation: Practice is of two kinds: one is right practice, and the other is mixed practice. As for right practice: to practice specifically in accordance with the rebirth scriptures (the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Amitābha Sutra, and the Sutra of Immeasurable Life) — this is right practice. What are the right practices? With a single mind, specifically to read and recite the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Amitābha Sutra, the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and so on; with a single mind, specifically to contemplate, observe, and recollect the glorious rewards of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. If bowing to the Buddha, then with a single mind specifically bow to Amitābha Buddha; if reciting aloud, then with a single mind specifically recite Amitābha Buddha; if praising and making offerings, then with a single mind specifically praise and make offerings; only this is called right practice. Further, within this right practice there are again two kinds: first, with a single mind specifically recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of the length of time, without letting go thought after thought (the thought of reciting the Buddha being unbroken — not cut off by sundry thoughts) — this is called the right conclusive karma, because it accords with Amitābha Buddha’s fundamental vow; if one relies on bowing, recitation, and so on, this is called sustaining karma. Apart from these right and sustaining practices, all other good deeds are called mixed practices. If one cultivates these right and sustaining practices, the mind is constantly drawn near to Amitābha Buddha, and recollection is never interrupted — this is called being without interruption (without the mingling of stray thoughts).
In this passage Master Shandao strongly emphasizes
a single mind
. Whether reciting scriptures, recollecting, bowing to the Buddha, upholding the name, or praising and making offerings,
one must
have a single mind
, because this is the
key
to correct practice!
A single mind
means thought following thought, without the intermingling of another thought.
The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu’s Treatise on Rebirth says:
O World-Honored One, I,
with a single mind
take refuge throughout the ten directions in the Tathāgata of Unobstructed Light, and wish to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.”
Master Tanluan, in his Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, explains:
The ‘I’
with a single mind
is the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu’s word of self-admonition. It means that, recollecting the Tathāgata of Unobstructed Light and wishing to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss,
thought follows thought, without the intermingling of another thought
Therefore, “a single mind” means thought following thought, without the intermingling of another thought.
[Tathāgata of Unobstructed Light]One of Amitābha Buddha’s twelve alternate names.
The Great Master Zhiyi said:
“If one applies the mind to keep the recollection,
thought following thought continuously
the other minds not interrupting
(not being interrupted by other thoughts)
therefore it is called a single mind
(From the Commentary on the Meaning of Guanyin)
A single mind is concentrating the mind on one thing, with no other thought,
which is what the Master Yongming, the reappearance of Amitābha Buddha, meant by “
free of all stray thoughts
(free of any other thought).” Master Yongming said:
“At the time of walking the path
(the meditative walk)
and paying homage, while reciting the Buddha and making the vow, with earnest and utmost sincerity,
free of all stray thoughts
, as one about to meet a death sentence, as one shut in a prison
(bì prison: a jail)
, pursued by hostile bandits, pressed by water and fire,
with a single mind

seeking deliverance, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly to realize the unborn, to liberate sentient beings widely, to continue and promote the Triple Gem, vowing to repay the four kinds of grace. With such wholehearted sincerity, what is done will surely not be in vain.”

(Translation: At the time of walking the path and paying homage, while reciting the Buddha and making the vow, with earnest and utmost sincerity, free of all stray thoughts, as one about to be executed, as one shut in a prison, as one pursued by hostile bandits, as one pressed by water and fire, urgently
with a single mind

seeking deliverance, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly to realize the unborn, to liberate sentient beings widely, to continue and promote the Triple Gem, vowing to repay the four kinds of grace. With such wholehearted sincerity, the effort is not in vain, and one will certainly be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.)
(From The Collection of Myriad Goods Returning to the One)

[Wheel of suffering]The suffering fruits of birth and death, turning like a wheel without resting. [The unborn]Neither born nor extinguished, that is, the principle of nirvāṇa. [Continue and promote]To carry on and spread forth. [Wholehearted sincerity]Earnest and single-minded.
Question: Why did Master Shandao copy more than one hundred thousand fascicles of the Amitābha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha?

Answer: At that time there was not yet any printing; the scriptures were all hand-copied and were rare and precious. In order that the many reciters of the Buddha’s name might all practice in accordance with the Amitābha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, as it teaches — faith, vow, and recitation of the name with single-minded undistracted concentration — he copied them and distributed them to the reciters. This also proves that Master Shandao did not maintain that “as long as there is faith, one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death,” but rather that the reciter ought to practice in accordance with the Amitābha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, as it teaches: faith, vow, and recitation of the name with single-minded undistracted concentration, and at the moment of death one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The four assemblies of disciples, moved by his influence, turned their minds to the Pure Land beyond all counting. Among Master Shandao’s disciples were those who recited the Amitābha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha from one hundred thousand up to five hundred thousand times, and those who took upon themselves a daily practice of the Buddha’s name from ten thousand up to one hundred thousand recitations; among them, those who attained the samādhi of Buddha-recitation and accomplished rebirth in the Pure Land cannot be enumerated.
Question: When the reciter is dying, Amitābha Buddha will naturally dispatch a boat to fetch him; why must one have single-minded undistracted concentration?

Answer: When the reciter is dying, there are seven boats that come to fetch him. One boat is for going to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and the other six are for the heavens, the human realm, the asura realm, the animal realm, the hungry-ghost realm, and the hell realm. The reason one must recite with single-minded undistracted concentration is that at the moment of death one may have clear right mindfulness and board the boat for the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore Master Shandao taught one to keep “
an uninterrupted recollection from thought to thought, making it the task of a lifetime
.” If one is able to keep “
an uninterrupted recollection from thought to thought, making it the task of a lifetime
,” then “
when the previous thought ends in death, the next thought is born immediately

.” If at the moment of death one is enveloped by delusion, then in the midst of delusion one will, following the pull of karma, board the boat among the six realms that corresponds to one’s own karma.(This is what the Master Yongming, the reappearance of Amitābha Buddha and sixth patriarch of the Pure Land school, says in the Four Selections: “The shadowy state suddenly appears before one, and in the blink of an eye one goes with it.”)If at death one recites the Buddha without delusion and without drowsiness, then it is the power of the vow that takes command, and one boards the boat for the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; this is the situation Master Shandao called “
when the previous thought ends in death, the next thought is born immediately
.” So Master Shandao earnestly admonished: “
May all people reflect deeply on this. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they must steel their minds and restrain themselves, and never neglect it by day or by night
,” and then there will be: “
when the previous thought ends in death, the next thought is born immediately. Forever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma-bliss, and even attaining Buddhahood — how joyful!

” This is also why Master Shandao copied more than one hundred thousand fascicles of the Amitābha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha and distributed them to the reciters, so that they would practice in accordance with the sutra as it teaches and attain single-minded undistracted concentration in recitation. In this way, at the moment of death, one would not be enveloped by delusion, but would board the boat for the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss with clear right mindfulness.
Question: As soon as faith is roused, one is reborn. What need is there for right mindfulness at death?
Answer: How can there be no need for right mindfulness at death? Master Shandao taught:
“When one is gravely ill and on the point of death, family members must not shed tears and wail, nor make sounds of sighing and regret that disturb the mind and spirit,
causing the loss of right mindfulness
. They should only, all at once, recite the Buddha in unison, and only after the breath is spent may they weep in grief.
If there is the slightest thought of attachment to the world, it becomes a hindrance, and there is no liberation

. If one can find people who clearly understand the Pure Land to come frequently and encourage one, this is an extremely great fortune. If one follows this method, one is certain to rise [to rebirth], without any doubt.”
(From
The Venerable Shandao’s Essay on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at Death
)In this Essay on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at Death, Master Shandao goes on to teach:

This method, used by monks, laypeople, or those who have not yet recited the Buddha, all attain rebirth — of this there is no doubt. I have often seen people in the world who, in ordinary life, recite the Buddha and praise [him], making the vow to seek rebirth in the West with great diligence
(earnest and sincere)
. Yet when illness comes upon them, they are again afraid of death, and say nothing at all about rebirth and liberation. They wait until the breath is spent and the life is ended,
consciousness having plunged into the spirit world
, and only then do they practice the ten recollections. This is exactly like closing the door after the thief has gone — of what use is it? The matter of birth and death is great;
one must exert oneself
. If a single thought goes astray, one suffers for kalpas upon kalpas — who can take one’s place? Think on this! Think on this! When there is nothing else to do, one should with this method
practice with vigor and uphold it
; this is the great matter of death.”
From this Essay on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at Death, we can clearly see Master Shandao’s guiding thought on Pure Land practice:
First, in order to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one must have right mindfulness at death; that is why the title is called “
Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at Death
Second, in order
to be able to ensure right mindfulness at death
, in ordinary life one must diligently cultivate,
achieving a recollection uninterrupted from thought to thought
; this is the foremost great matter for the reciter of the Buddha’s name.
Therefore, Master Shandao by no means maintained that “as long as the reciter has faith, he is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at the moment of death.” Rather, he maintained:

“Because reciting the name is easy, continuity brings immediate rebirth. If one can keep the recollection of the Buddha uninterrupted from thought to thought, making it the task of a lifetime, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred.

May all people reflect deeply on this. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they must steel their minds and restrain themselves, and never neglect it by day or by night; when the previous thought ends in death, the next thought is born immediately. Forever enjoying the unconditioned Dharma-bliss, and even attaining Buddhahood — how joyful!”

It is precisely because of the “uninterrupted recollection from thought to thought, making it the task of a lifetime” that one can ensure right mindfulness at death and be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Question: In Master Shandao’s Commentary on the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life(Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles)he says:

“With a single mind specifically reciting the name of Amitābha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of the length of time, without letting go thought after thought — this is called the right conclusive karma, because it accords with that Buddha’s vow.”
What is meant by “the right conclusive karma”?

Answer: karma (yè) carries the meaning of making and acting. Right samādhi (zhèngdìng) is correct concentration. When body and mind are pure and serene and one enters the undefiled samādhi, this is called “right samādhi.” “Undefiled” (wúlòu) means free of affliction. “Single-mindedly and exclusively calling on Amitabha Buddha’s name” means that the whole mind is fixed upon Amitabha’s name — only this is single-minded exclusive recitation. (If one keeps reciting the Buddha’s name while giving rise to scattered thoughts, then it is not single-minded exclusive recitation, but recitation with a divided and inconstant mind.) “Never letting go of the thought, thought after thought” (niàn niàn bù shě) means that the thought of the Buddha-recitation continues thought after thought, without any false thought mixed in between. (If one recites the Buddha’s name while giving rise to scattered thoughts, then it is not “never letting go thought after thought”; rather, as soon as a false thought arises, the Buddha-thought is set aside. How, then, could this be called right samādhi?)

The passage above is drawn from Master Shandao’s discussion of the right practice of a student of the Pure Land school (apart from this right practice, all the rest is sundry practice). Master Shandao taught:

“Yet practice is of two kinds: the first is right practice, the second is sundry practice. As for right practice, one who exclusively relies upon the scripture of rebirth and practices accordingly is called right practice. What is this?
Single-mindedly
recite this Visualization Sutra, the Amitabha Sutra, and the Immeasurable Life Sutra,
single-mindedly
contemplate, observe, and recollect the twofold glory of that land. If bowing, then
single-mindedly
bow to that Buddha; if calling aloud, then
single-mindedly
call upon that Buddha; if praising and making offerings, then
single-mindedly
praise and make offerings; this is called right practice. Further, within this right practice there are again two kinds: the first is
single-mindedly

reciting Amitabha’s name, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, without regard to how long the time, never letting go of it thought after thought — this is called the karmic act of right samādhi, because it accords with that Buddha’s vows; and if one relies upon bowing, reciting, and the like, these are called auxiliary karmic acts. Apart from these two practices of right and auxiliary, all the remaining good deeds are called sundry practice. If one cultivates the foregoing right and auxiliary practices, with the mind ever drawing near, recollecting without interruption, this is called unbroken practice.”
In this discourse, Master Shandao set forth the right practice and the auxiliary practice of a student of the Pure Land school with complete clarity,
and especially emphasized single-mindedness rather than a scattered mind.

So how can one say that Master Shandao advocated that “a person who recites the Buddha’s name need only have faith and, at the end of life, will immediately be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss”? Moreover, Master Shandao himself put it into practice: “Diligent, earnest, and painstaking, bowing and reciting day and night as if saving his head from a blaze. Each time he entered the chamber he knelt at length and chanted the Buddha’s name, never stopping until his strength was spent. Even in freezing weather he would chant until sweat soaked the collar of his robe before resting. When abroad he proclaimed the Pure Land teaching, and for more than thirty years he never lay down to sleep. He upheld the precepts without the slightest breach.” Not only that, Master Shandao also earnestly admonished:

“May all beings earnestly reflect: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must discipline the mind and restrain yourself, and neither by day nor night ever let slip. When the thoughts of the final thought cease, the next thought immediately arises. Eternally enjoying the unconditioned bliss of Dharma, even until reaching Buddhahood, is this not most joyful!”

How, then, can one say that Master Shandao advocated that “a person who recites the Buddha’s name need only have faith and, at the end of life, will immediately be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss”?
Question: The Sutra of the Buddha’s Teaching on Immeasurable Life says:

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings in the ten directions sincerely trust and rejoice, wishing to be born in my land, even with as few as ten thoughts — if they are not born there, may I not attain the highest enlightenment. Excepted only are those who commit the five grave offenses and slander the right Dharma.”
Therefore, as long as one truly believes, calling upon the Buddha’s name but ten times is enough to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss
— why then must one be single-minded and unperturbed?
Answer: In the sutra passage
“even as few as ten thoughts”

— if this refers to the ten recitations of daily life, then every reciter of the Buddha’s name would surely be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Does this accord with the actual experience of reciters who have been reborn in the Western Land over the past thousand years? If a mere ten recitations in daily life were enough to gain rebirth, why would the World-Honored One, in the
Sutra in Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Retaining Power
speak of
“keeping the mind fixed and unperturbed”
? And why must He repeatedly enjoin
“practicing as taught”
Therefore, the
“even as few as ten thoughts”
of the sutra refers to the
ten thoughts at the moment of death
and, moreover, to the
unbroken ten thoughts at death.
Since ancient times the patriarchs and great masters have analyzed this with great clarity (see the article
The Eighteenth Vow

). And Master Ouyi, in the preface to the Pure Land Repentance and Society for the Liberation of Beings in his Lingfeng Collected Works, stated: for the ten thoughts at death to arise, one must have planted deep roots of goodness, so that right thought can appear at the final moment. If, when favorable and adverse circumstances present themselves at present, one already no longer has right thought, how much less could one maintain right thought at death? Moreover, in broad daylight, with everything bright and clear, one still cannot accept and practice in faith the true admonitions and guidance of a wise teacher and good friend; how can one imagine that, at the time of death’s suffering, one could rely merely on a good friend’s reminder and teaching to accept and practice in faith? Furthermore, when death comes, how can one be certain that a true good friend will indeed appear? Even if a true good friend does appear, if the person’s consciousness is then clouded and confused, then to seek his faith and understanding is utterly impossible! (The original text reads: “For the ten thoughts at death, one must have deep roots of goodness. When favorable and adverse circumstances now arrive, one no longer has right thought, much less at death. Moreover, when suffering appears at death, one relies only on the admonition of a good friend; in broad daylight one still cannot accept and practice in faith the true words of a wise teacher and friend! When death comes, can one be sure a good friend will appear? Even if one appears and gives instruction, if the consciousness is clouded, to seek faith and understanding is thereby a thing utterly unattainable.”)
Moreover, Master Yongming was a manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, and his teaching on the
ten thoughts fulfilled at death
also proves that the “even as few as ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow in the Sutra of the Buddha’s Teaching on Immeasurable Life refer to the ten thoughts at the moment of death.
Master Yongming declared:
“While walking the path
(the circumambulation)
in the course of bowing in reverence, and at the time of reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows, with utmost earnestness and sincerity,
free of all idle thoughts
— like one going to execution, like one in a bìláo
(bìláo: a place of confinement)

— pursued by bandits and foes, pressed by flood and fire, with one mind crying out for deliverance, vowing to escape the wheel of suffering, swiftly to realize the unborn, to rescue living beings far and wide, to carry on the Three Jewels, and swearing to repay the fourfold grace. With such sincerity, one’s effort will never be wasted. But if words and deeds are inconsistent and the power of faith is slight, without
a mind of thought-after-thought continuity
and with a will that is interrupted again and again
(the thought of recitation being cut off by idle thoughts)
— relying on such negligence, hoping for rebirth at death, one is shrouded only by karmic hindrance and is unlikely to meet a good friend
(one fears it is hardly possible to meet a good friend able to arouse right thought at the end of life)
— when the wind and fire press upon one, right thought cannot be accomplished. Why?
Because the present is the cause and death is the fruit
; the cause must be real for the fruit not to be false. If one wishes
to have the ten thoughts fulfilled at death
, then prepare the ford and the bridge beforehand, gather up the merit, and dedicate it to that very time
(dedicating it to the time of death)
, so that no thought is deficient
(so that thought follows thought without interruption)
, then there is no more cause for anxiety.”
(from the Collection of the Ten Thousand Good Deeds Returning to One)

From this it is clear that rebirth through ten thoughts means the final ten thoughts at death, and rebirth through a single thought means the final single thought at death; the final determination at death is the truly real determination. At the moment of death it is like a person arriving at the airport: at ordinary times one speaks of going here and going there, but where one in the end goes depends wholly upon which aircraft one finally boards. Therefore, to be able, at the last moment of death, single-mindedly to recite ten phrases of the Buddha’s name or even a single phrase is of paramount importance. The reason one should be single-minded and unperturbed in daily recitation is precisely so that at the final moment one can single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name ten times, or even once.

As for the state of recitation of a person who has committed the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds yet is reborn through the ten thoughts at death, Master Yinguang instructed: although he has not personally realized single-mindedness and unperturbed peace, yet at death, apart from the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name, his mind is in the end wholly free of any other thought. (Master Yinguang’s original instruction reads:

“In the Visualization Sutra it is told that one who has committed the five grave offenses and the ten evil deeds, at the point of death, sees the signs of hell appear; a good friend (original note: here no distinction is made of monk, layperson, man, or woman — whoever can teach him to recite the Buddha’s name is called a good friend) teaches him to recite the Buddha’s name. Whether he recites but ten sounds or not even ten, and then straightway dies, he too may rely upon the Buddha’s compassionate power and be reborn while carrying his karma. These ten thoughts, compared with the ordinary ten thoughts, possess a ferocity and urgency as different as heaven and hell; hence he attains rebirth. Pressed by the extreme suffering of hell, once he hears the Buddha’s name, he invokes it with his whole being. Apart from this thought there is absolutely no other thought. Though he has not personally realized single-mindedness and unperturbed peace, his mind is in the end wholly free of any other thought.”
(from The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Third Compilation, Volume Two, Reply to Layman Chen Xinru.)
Question: The Sutra of the Buddha’s Teaching on Immeasurable Life says:

“All sentient beings who hear that Buddha’s name, with faith and joy, even for a single thought turn the mind back with all sincerity, wishing to be born in that land, shall thereupon be reborn there and dwell in the state of non-retrogression. Excepted only are those who commit the five grave offenses and slander the right Dharma.”
Thus, as long as one truly believes, turning the mind back with all sincerity but a single time is enough to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss
— why then must one be single-minded and unperturbed?

Answer: Within “even a single thought of sincere dedication,” the meaning of “single thought” (yī niàn) is: to single one’s mind. Hence “single thought of sincere dedication” means dedicating oneself, with the mind made single and undivided (without any stray thought), with all sincerity — and not “turning the mind back with all sincerity but a single time.” If one understands it as: by turning the mind back with all sincerity but once one is straightway reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, then does such an understanding hold up? Does it accord with the actual circumstances of rebirth?

In sum, “as long as one truly believes, calling upon the Buddha’s name but ten times is enough to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss,” and “as long as one truly believes, turning the mind back with all sincerity but once is enough to be reborn there” — do these accord with the actual rebirth of those among the reciters of the Buddha’s name? The Sutra of the Buddha’s Teaching on Immeasurable Life says:

“One ascends the path without limit; easy it is to go, yet none goes. That land turns none away; beings are drawn on by their own nature. Why not abandon worldly affairs and diligently practice, seeking the Way and virtue? So may one gain the utmost long life, with bliss that has no end.”
Has your so-called “true faith” accomplished
“Why not abandon worldly affairs and diligently practice, seeking the Way and virtue”
? Have you accomplished the Buddha’s admonition in the words that follow? The Buddha said:

“I now tell you that because of worldly affairs people sit and fail to attain the Way. You should think it over with care and stay far from all evil. Choose what is good and diligently practice it. Love, desire, honor, and splendor cannot be kept forever; all must be parted from, and there is nothing in them to delight in. In this world when a Buddha appears,
one should be diligent and vigorous.
Those who have a most earnest vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss may attain wisdom, clarity, and penetrating understanding, with merit superlative.
Do not follow one’s own desires, fail the sutra’s precepts, and linger behind others.
Question: What is the meaning of “That land turns none away; beings are drawn on by their own nature”?
Answer: The meaning of “that land turns none away; beings are drawn on by their own nature” in the sutra is this: the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss does not reject any being (
that land turns none away

); but the reason beings cannot be reborn there is that at the end of their lives they are unable to maintain right thought, so that the circumstance of the intermediate state appears, and they go with their karmic power to take rebirth in the six realms, wholly without the power to direct themselves (
drawn on by their own nature

). To this, Master Lianchi, in his Commentarial Digest on the Amitabha Sutra, taught: those who are inverted at death are all those who, in daily life, follow their random thoughts, do not cultivate right thought, and have minds much scattered. At the moment the four elements separate, the deeds of a lifetime all appear before them; the mind is terrified and the bearing is thrown into disorder. One who is to enter hell takes the mountain of knives and the forest of swords to be a beautiful garden. One who is to fall among the animals takes the belly of a horse and the womb of a donkey to be a splendid hall. Even one who has done good and should be born among humans or devas, at the moment of entering the womb, cannot avoid loving the mother and hating the father and so becoming male, or loving the father and hating the mother and so becoming female. Even one who has reached the first fruit of the Lesser Vehicle, or a bodhisattva newly arisen in aspiration, still has the delusion of the intermediate state and cannot enter and leave the womb with right knowledge. These are all inversions. Because of the inversion at death, within the three realms and the seven destinies,
beings take rebirth according to their karma
. (The original text:

“Those who are inverted at death, by following random thoughts in daily life, do not cultivate right thought, and have minds much scattered. When about to relinquish the warmth and touch of the body, the deeds of a whole life all appear before them; the mind is terrified and confused, and movement and stillness are thrown into disorder. One who is to enter hell takes the mountain of knives and the forest of swords to be a garden. One who is to fall among the animals takes the belly of a horse and the womb of a donkey for a hall. Even one who does good and ought to be reborn among humans and devas cannot escape loving and hating parents. Even a lesser sage newly arisen in mind cannot know rightly its going out and coming in. These are all what are called the inversions. Riding upon this inversion, within the three realms and seven destinies, beings take rebirth according to their karma.”
[Seven Destinies] hell, hungry ghosts, beasts, humans, immortals, devas, and asuras. “Destiny” (qù) means the direction toward which one goes.
